clinicalPearls: The most common extracranial solid tumour of childhood and the most common malignancy of infancy, arising from primitive sympathetic neural crest cells.
It can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain; the adrenal medulla and paraspinal abdomen are the most frequent primary sites.
An abdominal primary often presents as a firm, irregular mass that crosses the midline, distinguishing it from Wilms tumour.
Presentation is highly variable and may include systemic upset, bone pain, proptosis with periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes') from orbital metastases, or a paraspinal mass causing cord compression.
Distinctive paraneoplastic features include opsoclonus-myoclonus (dancing eyes, dancing feet) and secretory diarrhoea from vasoactive intestinal peptide.
Most tumours secrete catecholamines, so urinary homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) are useful markers.
Behaviour spans a remarkable spectrum, from spontaneous regression in infants (including stage MS/4S disease) to aggressive, widely metastatic disease.
MYCN amplification is a key adverse biological marker that upstages risk and intensifies therapy.
Risk stratification integrating age, stage, histology, and genetics guides treatment ranging from observation or surgery to intensive multimodal therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Neuroblastoma develops from neural crest-derived precursors of the sympathetic nervous system, giving rise to a spectrum from undifferentiated neuroblastoma to more mature ganglioneuroblastoma and benign ganglioneuroma. Tumour behaviour is strongly governed by biology: MYCN amplification, segmental chromosomal changes, and DNA ploidy correlate with aggressiveness, while some infant tumours undergo differentiation or apoptosis and regress spontaneously.
additionalDifferentials: Ewing sarcoma / other small round blue cell tumours
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of the primary site
MIBG scintigraphy for functional imaging and metastasis detection
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for marrow involvement
Tumour biopsy for histology and biology including MYCN status
Full blood count, renal and liver function, lactate dehydrogenase and ferritin
redFlags: Signs of spinal cord compression from a paraspinal (dumbbell) tumour
Rapidly progressive or widely metastatic disease
Periorbital bruising and proptosis suggesting orbital metastases
Severe secretory diarrhoea from a VIP-secreting tumour
Systemic deterioration with bone pain and marrow failure
reference.prognosis: Outcome is extremely variable: low-risk and infant disease (including 4S/MS) often has excellent survival and may regress, whereas high-risk disease with MYCN amplification or widespread metastases has a much poorer prognosis despite intensive therapy.
pitfalls: Confusing it with Wilms tumour when it presents as an abdominal mass
Missing spinal cord compression from a paraspinal component
Overlooking opsoclonus-myoclonus as a paraneoplastic clue to occult tumour
Failing to obtain MYCN status, which changes management
Assuming all disease is aggressive and over-treating low-risk or regressing tumours
